gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long hiss you can hold for as long as you like — 'sssss', not 'suh'. Don't let a vowel sneak onto the end.
gpcs.mnemonic: Sula the snail slides along so slowly, leaving a soft 'sss' trail behind her wherever she goes.

character.name: Sula
character.blurb: Sula is a gentle garden snail who never rushes, always leaving a shining trail as she hisses her way along the path.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top right. Curve up and round to the left, then across and back round to the right, and round to the left at the bottom. Finish at the bottom left.
gpcs.action: Trace a slow wavy line in the air with one finger while whispering a long 'sssss', following the shape of Sula's trail.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, flat sound made with the mouth open wide — 'a' as in 'cat', not the long letter name.
gpcs.mnemonic: Acer the acorn drops from the branch and bounces on the ground three times — 'a, a, a'!

character.name: Acer
character.blurb: Acer is a small round acorn with a fuzzy little cap who loves to bounce down from the tallest branch.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and all the way back up to where you started, then go straight down without lifting. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Crouch down and spring up a tiny bit three times, like Acer bouncing on the ground, saying 'a, a, a'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A quick, light tap of the tongue behind the top teeth — 't', not 'tuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Tolly the feather taps gently on the twig every time the wind blows — 't, t, t'.

character.name: Tolly
character.blurb: Tolly is a light little feather who loves to rest on twigs and tap out a soft beat when the breeze catches him.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start a little above the small letters. Pull straight down and finish on the line with a small curve to the right. Lift, then draw a short line across at the top of the small letters, from left to right.
gpcs.action: Tap one fingertip lightly on the back of your other hand twice, like Tolly tapping the twig, saying 't, t'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A little puff of air as closed lips pop open — 'p', not 'puh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Poppy the pinecone pops open one scale at a time in the warm sun — 'p, p, p'.

character.name: Poppy
character.blurb: Poppy is a tightly closed pinecone who loves warm, sunny days because that's when her scales pop open one by one.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down below the line, go back up the same line, then curve round to the right and back. Finish where the curve meets the line.
gpcs.action: Press your lips together and let them pop open softly with a little puff of air, like one of Poppy's scales popping, saying 'p, p'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, quick sound — 'i' as in 'sit', not the long letter name 'eye'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Iggy the raindrop drips off the leaf tip in a hurry — 'i, i, i' — plip, plip, plip.

character.name: Iggy
character.blurb: Iggy is a tiny, speedy raindrop who never sits still for long, always dripping quickly from leaf to leaf.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down and finish on the line. Lift, and add a dot above.
gpcs.action: Give one quick, tiny tap on top of your head with a fingertip, like a drop landing, saying a short 'i'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A gentle hum through the nose with the tongue behind the top teeth — 'n', not 'nuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Nettie the nest hums softly as her baby birds settle down to sleep — 'n, n, n'.

character.name: Nettie
character.blurb: Nettie is a cosy woven nest tucked into a hedge, with one twig always sticking out at a funny angle.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up the same line, then over in a hump and down. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Cup both hands together in front of your chest like a small nest and hum a gentle 'nnn', tongue tip behind your top teeth.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A closed-lip hum held for a moment — 'mmm', not 'muh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Milo the mushroom hums happily under the shady tree all day long — 'mmm, mmm'.

character.name: Milo
character.blurb: Milo is a round, spotty mushroom who loves cool, shady corners of the garden and hums to himself all day.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up, over in a hump and down, back up and over in a second hump and down. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Press your lips together and hum a long 'mmm' while patting both cheeks gently, like Milo humming to himself.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A firm, quick tap of the tongue just behind the top teeth — 'd', not 'duh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Dara the duckling dips her beak into the pond three times — 'd, d, d'.

character.name: Dara
character.blurb: Dara is a bright golden duckling who loves dipping her beak into the pond to look for pondweed.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and back up to where you started, keep going straight up to make a tall line, then come straight back down it without lifting. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Dip your head forward and down quickly, like Dara dipping for pondweed, saying 'd, d'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A soft sound made at the back of the throat — 'g' as in 'got', not 'guh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Gigi the egg wobbles gently from side to side — 'g, g, g' — rocking but never falling.

character.name: Gigi
character.blurb: Gigi is a speckled egg tucked safely in a nest, who loves to rock gently from side to side.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and back up to where you started, then go straight down below the line and curl round to the left. Finish below the line.
gpcs.action: Rock gently from side to side on the spot, like Gigi wobbling in her nest, saying 'g, g'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, round sound made with rounded lips — 'o' as in 'dog', not the long letter name.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ozzy the owl opens his big round eyes wide and hoots — 'o, o, o'.

character.name: Ozzy
character.blurb: Ozzy is a round-eyed owl with two little feather tufts, who blinks slowly and loves the quiet of night.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top. Curve round to the left, down, round the bottom and back up. Finish where you started, closing the circle.
gpcs.action: Make two round circles with your thumbs and fingers and hold them up to your eyes like Ozzy's, saying 'o, o'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, sharp sound from the back of the throat — 'c' as in 'cat', not 'cuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Coco the caterpillar curls up small on a leaf — 'c, c, c' — curling a little tighter each time.

character.name: Coco
character.blurb: Coco is a striped caterpillar who loves to curl into a tight little ball whenever she feels shy.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top right. Curve up, over to the left, round and down. Finish at the bottom right, leaving the c open.
gpcs.action: Curl one hand slowly into a loose fist, like Coco curling up, saying a short 'c'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: The same sharp sound as 'c' — a quick, short 'k', not 'kuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Kip the acorn lands on the path and cracks his cap with a sharp little click — 'k, k, k'.

character.name: Kip
character.blurb: Kip is a fresh acorn who has just fallen from the tree, and his cap always clicks when he lands.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line and pull straight down. Finish on the line. Lift, start at the top right of the small letters, slant in to touch the tall line, then slant out. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Tap one knuckle sharply on the table or your knee once, like Kip's cap cracking, saying 'k'.

trickyWords.tip: On its own this letter keeps its short /a/ sound, as in 'cat'. The tricky part: in a sentence we say it quickly and softly, like 'uh' — 'a cat' sounds like 'uh cat'.
The 's' at the end says /z/, not its usual hissy sound — listen for 'iz'.
You'll spot 'the' everywhere in a story — the tricky bit is the ending, which says a quick 'thuh' instead of the 'eh' sound e usually makes.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one sharp sound — 'ck' says exactly the same as 'k', usually at the end of short words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Kester the duckling snaps his beak shut quickly whenever he hears a click — 'ck, ck'.

character.name: Kester
character.blurb: Kester is a quick, alert duckling with a tuft of down on his head, always the first to snap his beak at a passing fly.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'c', then 'k', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Clap your hands together once, sharply and quickly, like Kester's beak snapping shut, saying 'ck'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, flat sound — 'e' as in 'egg', not the long letter name.
gpcs.mnemonic: Elsie the flower trembles her petals in the breeze — 'e, e, e'.

character.name: Elsie
character.blurb: Elsie is a bright, striped-petal flower who quivers gently whenever the smallest breeze passes by.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start on the left, halfway up the small letters. Go straight across to the right, then curve up, over and round to the left and along the bottom. Finish at the bottom right.
gpcs.action: Give your fingers a tiny flutter near your chest, like Elsie's petals trembling, saying a short 'e'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, quick sound from the middle of the mouth — 'u' as in 'sun', not 'yoo'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Una the butterfly dips down low, then lifts up, up, up into the air — 'u, u, u'.

character.name: Una
character.blurb: Una is a spotted butterfly who loves to dip down to a flower before lifting straight back up into the sky.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull down, curve round the bottom and up to the top, then straight back down. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Scoop both hands from your waist up to your shoulders, like Una lifting off, saying a short 'u'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A growly sound you can hold, 'rrr', with the tongue pulled back and not touching the roof of the mouth — not rolled, and not 'ruh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Rusty the robin ruffles his feathers and growls out a proud 'rrr' from his branch.

character.name: Rusty
character.blurb: Rusty is a proud little robin with a bright red-berry chest who loves to ruffle his feathers before he sings.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up the same line, then curve over to the right. Finish just past the top of the line.
gpcs.action: Give your shoulders a quick shimmy, like Rusty ruffling his feathers, while making a soft growly 'rrr'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A soft breath out with no sound from the throat — just breathe out 'h', don't add 'huh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Hazel the hedgehog puffs out a breathy 'h, h, h' every time she curls into a tight little ball.

character.name: Hazel
character.blurb: Hazel is a small sandy-brown hedgehog with one stray tuft of fur, who always puffs before she curls up to sleep.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down, go back up part of the way, then over in a hump and down. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Cup your hands loosely near your mouth and breathe out softly, 'h, h', like warming cold hands, the way Hazel puffs before curling up.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, bouncy sound with closed lips popping open — 'b', not 'buh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Bud the bee bumps gently against the flower petals — 'b, b, b' — before she lands.

character.name: Bud
character.blurb: Bud is a round, striped bee who always bumps softly against a flower bud before settling down to land.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down, go back up part of the way, then curve round to the right and back. Finish at the bottom of the line.
gpcs.action: Tap your chest once, gently, with a closed fist, like Bud bumping a petal, saying 'b'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, steady hiss made with the top teeth resting on the bottom lip — 'ffff', not 'fuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Fennel the feather floats down slowly, the air hissing softly past her — 'ffff'.

character.name: Fennel
character.blurb: Fennel is a slender, striped feather who loves to drift on the breeze, taking her time to reach the ground.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start a little below the top, on the right. Curve up and over to the left, then pull straight down. Finish on the line. Lift, then draw a short line across at the top of the small letters, from left to right.
gpcs.action: Rest your top teeth gently on your bottom lip and blow a long, slow 'ffff', like the breeze carrying Fennel down.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one long sound — 'ff' says exactly the same steady hiss as single 'f'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Fluff the cloud puffs herself along the sky with one long, steady breath — 'ffff'.

character.name: Fluff
character.blurb: Fluff is a soft, wide cloud who moves across the sky by puffing herself gently forward.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'f' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Puff both cheeks out and blow one long, slow 'ffff', like Fluff drifting all the way across the sky.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A clear, light sound with the tongue tip touching just behind the top teeth — 'l', not 'luh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Lila the leaf lets go of her branch and glides down long and smooth — 'llll'.

character.name: Lila
character.blurb: Lila is a slim, gently veined leaf who takes her time drifting all the way down from the highest branch.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Raise one arm straight up, then lower it slowly and smoothly, like Lila drifting down, saying a long 'llll'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one clear sound — 'll' says exactly the same as single 'l', often at the end of short words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Lottie and Lacey the ladybirds perch side by side on a tall blade of grass, both humming a long 'llll' together.

character.name: Lottie & Lacey
character.blurb: Lottie and Lacey are two spotty ladybirds who go everywhere together, always perching side by side.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'l' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Hold up two fingers side by side, like Lottie and Lacey together, and say one long 'llll'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one long hiss — 'ss' says exactly the same as single 's', often at the end of short words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Silva and Sable the snails race side by side, each leaving a long hissing trail — 'ssss'.

character.name: Silva & Sable
character.blurb: Silva and Sable are two garden snails who love a slow race, always finishing exactly side by side.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 's' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Trace two wavy trails in the air at once, one with each hand, while hissing a long 'ssss', like Silva and Sable racing.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Pure sound only, e.g. 'j-j-j' not 'juh' — keep it short and bouncy, no vowel on the end.
gpcs.mnemonic: Jem the ladybird jiggles and jumps, j-j-j, every time she lands on a leaf.

character.name: Jem
character.blurb: Jem is a small ladybird who can't stand still — she jiggles her wings before every little jump.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down below the line and curl round to the left. Finish below the line. Lift, and add a dot above.
gpcs.action: Give two quick jiggling jumps on the spot, elbows tucked in, saying j-j-j as you land each time.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A buzzy, continuous sound — top teeth rest gently on bottom lip and you can hold it, 'vvvv', don't add 'uh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Vela the vole feels her whiskers vibrate, vvv, whenever she trundles her tiny cart of seeds.

character.name: Vela
character.blurb: Vela is a round little hedgehog who pulls a cart everywhere, whiskers buzzing as the wheels turn.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Slant down to a point on the line, then slant up to the right. Finish at the top right.
gpcs.action: Rest two fingers lightly on your chin and let them 'buzz' while you hum vvv.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Round your lips into a small circle before you start, then open them as you say 'w' — quick and rounded, not stretched.
gpcs.mnemonic: Willow the wren wobbles side to side along her branch, w-w-w, before she takes off.

character.name: Willow
character.blurb: Willow is a small wren who never flies straight off — she wobbles a wiggly little dance on the branch first.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Slant down to a point, up to the middle, down to a second point, then up. Finish at the top right.
gpcs.action: Round your lips into a circle, sway your shoulders side to side twice, then say w-w-w.

trickyWords.tip: In 'to' the o makes a long 'oo' sound instead of its short sound — think of it as a tiny pointing word, always heading off to somewhere.
Sound out p-u-t. The tricky part is the u: in 'put' it says a short /oo/, as in 'book' (in many accents). Say it the way your class says it.
'I' is only one letter but it's always written tall as a capital, and it says its own name rather than the short i sound, because it means me — the person talking.
You've only learned the short o so far, like in 'dog', but in 'no' the o says its long name 'oh' instead — two letters for one big, definite word.
Just like 'is', the 's' at the end says /z/ — it rhymes with 'fizz', not with 'hiss'.
The 's' at the end says /z/ again — is, his and has all share this same trick, so learn them as a family.
Just like 'no', the o in 'go' says its long name 'oh' rather than the short sound from 'dog' — picture the two letters setting off on a journey.
The 'f' here says /v/, not its usual sound — say it out loud and you'll hear 'ov', not 'off'.
Sound out a-s. The tricky part is the s at the end: it says /z/, so 'as' sounds like 'az' — the same trick as is, his and has.
Once you know 'in' and 'to', you already know 'into' — just listen for the o at the end saying 'oo', not its short sound.

A name. Sound out O-l-i-v. The tricky part is the e at the end: it makes no sound. It is there because English words hardly ever end in v. In Year 1, children learn 've' as a spelling and can read Olive's name with no tricky part.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is two sounds squashed together, 'k' then 's' — say them fast, one after the other: ks.
gpcs.mnemonic: Xander the fox crosses his front paws, ks-ks, when he's about to pounce.

character.name: Xander
character.blurb: Xander is a cheeky little creature who always crosses his paws over each other before he moves.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters and slant down to the right. Finish on the line. Lift, start at the top right and slant down to the left, crossing the first line. Finish on the line.
gpcs.action: Cross your arms in front of your chest like an X while saying ks-ks.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A quick sound made at the front of the mouth, 'y-y-y' — don't turn it into 'yuh'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Yolanda the young duckling yawns and yelps, y-y-y, first thing every morning by the pond.

character.name: Yolanda
character.blurb: Yolanda is the youngest duckling in her family and always the first one awake, calling out to everyone else.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters and slant down to the right, to the line. Lift, start at the top right and slant down to the left, through the first line and on below it. Finish below the line.
gpcs.action: Cup your hands round your mouth like a little beak and call out y-y-y.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A buzzing sound you can hold, 'zzzz' — feel it tickle your lips, don't add 'uh' on the end.
gpcs.mnemonic: Zinnia the bee zigzags between the flowers, zzz, never flying in a straight line.

character.name: Zinnia
character.blurb: Zinnia is a busy little bee who always flies in quick zigzags instead of a straight path.

gpcs.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Go straight across to the right, slant down to the bottom left, then straight across to the right. Finish at the bottom right.
gpcs.action: Trace a zigzag in the air with one finger while buzzing zzz.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Still just one buzzing 'zzzz' sound even though it's written with two letters — hold it, don't say it twice.
gpcs.mnemonic: When Zinnia the bee gets excited she buzzes extra loud, zzzz, wings a blur.

character.name: Zinnia
character.blurb: Zinnia doubles her buzz when she's excited — one zigzag wing-beat just isn't enough.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'z' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Shake both hands fast by your ears like buzzing wings and hold zzzz.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Two sounds squashed together, 'k' then 'w' — say them fast as one: kw. These two letters are never split up.
gpcs.mnemonic: Quinn the quail quivers her tail feathers, kw-kw, whenever she's asking a question.

character.name: Quinn
character.blurb: Quinn is a curious little bird who quivers her tail whenever something puzzles her.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'q': start at the top right of a small round shape, curve round to the left and back up, then pull straight down below the line and finish there. Then write 'u' close beside it. 'q' is always followed by 'u'.
gpcs.action: Tilt your head to one side like you're puzzled and give a little shiver, saying kw-kw.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: One quick sound made together, 'ch' — like a small sneeze, don't say 'c' and 'h' apart.
gpcs.mnemonic: Chip the squirrel chomps his acorn in one quick bite, ch-ch, cheeks full.

character.name: Chip
character.blurb: Chip isn't a squirrel himself but the acorn he guards — he squeaks a sharp ch-ch whenever anyone tries to chomp him.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'c', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Snap your fingers once close to your mouth like a quick chomp, saying ch-ch.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A soft, quiet sound you can hold, 'shhh' — like asking for quiet, no vowel added on the end.
gpcs.mnemonic: Shelly the snail slides into her shell and whispers shhh when the garden gets too noisy.

character.name: Shelly
character.blurb: Shelly is a shy snail who tucks into her shell and hushes everyone with a soft shhh.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 's', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Hold one finger up to your lips and whisper shhh.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Pop your tongue tip gently between your teeth and blow, 'th' — it can sound soft (thin) or buzzy (that), practise both.
gpcs.mnemonic: Theo the tortoise pokes his tongue out just a little, th-th, whenever he's thinking hard.

character.name: Theo
character.blurb: Theo isn't a tortoise but a slow, thoughtful mushroom who pokes a little tongue-shaped frill out when he's puzzling something over.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 't', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Poke your tongue tip gently between your teeth and blow softly, th-th.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A hum made at the back of the mouth, 'ng' — like the end of 'sing', hold it and feel your nose buzz slightly.
gpcs.mnemonic: Nigel the nest hums a long, low ng-ng note that wobbles the twigs around him.

character.name: Nigel
character.blurb: Nigel is a cosy nest that hums a low ng note whenever the wind rocks him gently.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'n', then 'g', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Hum ng-ng with your mouth slightly open and the back of your tongue raised, and tap your nose gently to feel it buzz.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, gliding sound, 'ai' as in 'rain' — let it stretch, it slides from one shape to another.
gpcs.mnemonic: Acorn Ada waits under the leaf, chin up, whenever the first raindrop of a shower slides down, ai-ai.

character.name: Ada
character.blurb: Ada is a patient little acorn who tips her cap up to catch the first drops of rain.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'i', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Tip your chin up and trace one finger sliding down through the air like a raindrop, saying ai-ai.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, stretched sound, 'ee' as in 'tree' — smile as you say it and hold it for a full breath.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ellie the owl stretches up tall on her branch to see far and wide, ee-ee.

character.name: Ellie
character.blurb: Ellie is a curious owl who stretches her neck up long and tall whenever she's trying to see something far away.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'e' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Stretch your neck up tall, hands framing wide eyes, and hold ee-ee for a full breath.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long gliding sound, 'igh' as in 'night' — three letters, one sound, glide from a wide mouth to a smile.
gpcs.mnemonic: Isla the owl blinks her big eyes wide open at night, igh-igh, when the sky turns dark.

character.name: Isla
character.blurb: Isla is a night-time owl whose eyes go extra wide and round as soon as the sky darkens.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'g', then 'h', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Open your eyes wide like an owl and glide one hand upward through the air, saying igh-igh.

trickyWords.tip: The 'e' says its long name 'ee' instead of a short sound — point at a boy in a picture and say 'he is...' to link the word to its meaning.
Just like 'he' with 'sh' on the front — the 'e' says 'ee', so sound out sh-ee and blend it smoothly.
A tiny two-letter word where 'e' says 'ee' — link hands with a friend and say 'we' together to make it stick.
The 'e' says 'ee' again here — tap your own chest gently when you say 'me' so the word matches the action.
Another short word where 'e' says its name 'ee' — notice it rhymes with he, she, we and me, so they're easy to spot as a family.
The main tricky part is the 'a', which says /o/; the 's' also sounds like 'z', not 's' — say 'woz' quietly to yourself as a clue, then write 'was'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, rounded sound, 'oa' as in 'boat' — round your lips into an O shape and let it glide.
gpcs.mnemonic: Otto the duckling floats along, round and steady, oa-oa, wherever the pond takes him.

character.name: Otto
character.blurb: Otto is a calm little duckling who floats in a slow, steady circle no matter how choppy the pond gets.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'a', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Round your lips into an O, rock gently side to side like floating, and say oa-oa.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, deep sound, 'oo' as in 'moon' — round your lips small and hold it, this is the LONG version of oo.
gpcs.mnemonic: Luna the owl hoots a long, deep call across the moonlit garden, oo-oo.

character.name: Luna
character.blurb: Luna only hoots at night, a long deep oo-oo call that carries right across the garden.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Cup your hands around your mouth and hoot a long, low oo-oo.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, light sound, 'oo' as in 'book' — quick and soft, this is the SHORT version, different from the long 'oo' in 'moon'. The two 'oo' sounds are easy to mix up: one holds long (moon), this one is quick and clipped (book).
gpcs.mnemonic: Bobbin the hedgehog gives a quick, soft puff, oo-oo, when he's pushing a heavy pinecone.

character.name: Bobbin
character.blurb: Bobbin is a small, huffing hedgehog who gives short, quick puffs whenever he's pushing something heavy.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o' twice, close together, just like the long 'oo' — the letters are exactly the same, only the sound is different.
gpcs.action: Give a quick, soft puff of breath, oo-oo, like you're pushing something heavy just twice.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, open sound, 'ar' as in 'car' — open your mouth wide and let it drop back, hold it for a moment.
gpcs.mnemonic: Arlo the fox opens his mouth wide and lets out a long, low ar-ar under the starry sky.

character.name: Arlo
character.blurb: Arlo is a bright evening star who lets out a long, low twinkle-sound whenever the sky goes dark.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Open your mouth wide, tip your head back to look at the sky, and hold ar-ar.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, rounded sound, 'or' as in 'for' — round your lips more than 'ar' and hold it steady.
gpcs.mnemonic: Orin the owl rounds his beak into a small O and calls a long or-or before he swoops down.

character.name: Orin
character.blurb: Orin always rounds his beak into a tiny O shape and gives a long or-or call before he ever swoops.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Round your lips into a small O, mime swooping one arm downward, and say or-or.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A long, low sound made in the middle of the mouth, 'ur' as in 'burn' — lips slightly rounded, hold it steady like a purr.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ursula the hedgehog curls into a tight ball and hums a low, steady ur-ur while she rests.

character.name: Ursula
character.blurb: Ursula curls into a tight round ball whenever she's resting and hums a low, steady note.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Hug your arms around yourself like curling into a ball and hum a low, steady ur-ur.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A loud, gliding sound, 'ow' as in 'cow' — start wide and glide down, like a little yelp of surprise.
gpcs.mnemonic: Otis the owl flaps out and hoots a loud, surprised ow-ow when a branch wobbles under him.

character.name: Otis
character.blurb: Otis gives a startled ow-ow hoot whenever his branch wobbles unexpectedly beneath him.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Throw both arms out wide as if wobbling off balance and yelp ow-ow.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A short, sharp gliding sound, 'oi' as in 'coin' — start rounded and glide quickly to a smile, like calling out.
gpcs.mnemonic: Oskar the caterpillar bumps into a shiny leaf and calls out a sharp oi-oi in surprise.

character.name: Oskar
character.blurb: Oskar bumps into things more than any other caterpillar and always calls out a sharp oi-oi.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'i', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Throw one hand up like calling out to a friend and say a sharp oi-oi.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'ear' as in 'hear' — start short and glide gently towards 'uh', like leaning in to listen.
gpcs.mnemonic: Edie the sparrow leans in close and tilts her head, ear-ear, whenever a sound is far away.

character.name: Edie
character.blurb: Edie is a sharp-eared sparrow who tilts her head and leans in close to catch quiet, faraway sounds.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'a', then 'r', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Cup a hand behind your ear and lean your head in gently, saying ear-ear.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'air' as in 'chair' — start open and glide gently towards 'uh', let your voice float.
gpcs.mnemonic: Amara the feather drifts on the breeze, floating and swaying, air-air, before it lands.

character.name: Amara
character.blurb: Amara is a light feather who never falls straight down — she always drifts and sways on the air first.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'i', then 'r', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Hold one hand up like a feather and let it drift side to side slowly through the air, saying air-air.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'ure' as in 'sure' — lips rounded to start, gliding gently towards 'uh', soft and short.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ursa the snail tucks in sure and steady, ure-ure, whenever her shell feels safe and snug.

character.name: Ursa
character.blurb: Ursa only ever moves when she's sure it's safe, tucking snug into her shell with a soft ure-ure hum.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'r', then 'e', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Wrap your arms around yourself in a snug hug and hum ure-ure.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: 'er' as in 'her' and 'fern' — a steady sound like 'ur'. At the end of a longer word, as in 'hammer', it is lighter and quicker.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ember the mushroom mutters a soft, quiet er-er whenever a raindrop taps her cap.

character.name: Ember
character.blurb: Ember is a quiet mushroom who only ever mutters her sound softly, never loudly, whenever it rains.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Shrug your shoulders lightly and mutter a soft, quick er-er.

trickyWords.tip: The 'y' at the end makes the long 'igh' sound instead of a usual 'y' sound — point to something that belongs to you and say 'my' to anchor the meaning.
The 'y' says its usual sound, but 'ou' says a long 'oo' instead of its usual sound — point to a friend when you say it to help it stick.
The 'ey' ending makes a long 'ai' sound, not two separate sounds — practise it alongside 'grey' so the pattern feels familiar.
This one actually does sound out with the 'er' sound you already know — the tricky part is remembering when to use 'her' instead of 'she'.
The 'a' sounds like 'or' here, not its usual short sound — spread your arms out wide when you say 'all' to remember it means everything.
The letters don't sound out the way you'd expect for a short word — it rhymes with 'car' and 'star', so borrow that 'ar' sound to help remember it.
The 'ai' in the middle doesn't make its usual sound here — it says /e/ instead. Read the whole word together, then notice the 'ai' bit is the odd one out.
The 'a' says its short sound but the word still ends in an 'e' that isn't doing its usual job — most silent-e words stretch the vowel before it, this one just doesn't.
Sound out l and k. The tricky part is the 'i' and the 'e' at the end, which work together to make the 'i' say its name. Remember that part.
The single letter 'o' at the end says its own name, 'oh', all by itself — not every long 'o' sound needs two letters.
The 'o' here doesn't say 'oh' or its short sound — it says 'oo', like in 'zoo'. Listen carefully, it's easy to guess the wrong sound.
The 'o' says /u/ here, not its usual sound, and the 'e' on the end is silent and does nothing — say it out loud a few times so it sticks.
Just like 'some', the 'o' says /u/ instead of its usual sound — these two words are good friends, they rhyme even though they don't look like they should.

structures.label: CVCC words
structures.title: Two consonant sounds together at the end
structures.explanation: Words that end with two consonant sounds, like tent and milk. Say every sound, then blend: t-e-n-t, tent. Do not squash the last two sounds into one.

structures.label: CCVC words
structures.title: Two consonant sounds together at the start
structures.explanation: Words that start with two consonant sounds, like stop and frog. Say every sound, then blend: s-t-o-p, stop. For a sound you can hold (s, f, l), hold it and slide into the next one.

structures.label: CCVCC words
structures.title: Two consonant sounds at the start and two at the end
structures.explanation: Both skills in one word: crisp, trust, frost. Say every sound, left to right, then blend.

structures.label: Two-syllable words
structures.title: Longer words with two syllables
structures.explanation: Clap the two beats first (sand-pit), read each chunk sound by sound, then put the chunks together.

trickyWords.tip: The 'e' here says /er/, not its short sound — it looks like it should rhyme with 'here' but it actually rhymes with 'her'.
This word looks like 'here' with a 't' on the front, but say it out loud — the middle sounds like 'air', not 'ear'. Spot the matching shape, then listen for the different sound.
The ending 'le' says /ul/, a pattern that turns up at the end of lots of words — practise the whole ending as one chunk rather than sounding each letter.
This word doesn't look anything like it sounds — there's no /w/ letter to see, yet that's the very first sound you say. Just learn its shape by heart.
The 'wh' at the start says the same sound as a plain 'w' — listen for one /w/ sound, not two separate ones.
The letters 'ou' together make one sound, not two — say it like the sound you make when you're hurt, 'ow', then add the 't'.
The 'a' says /o/ here instead of its usual short sound — 'what' rhymes with 'hot', not with 'hat', even though it doesn't look like it should.

structures.label: With sh, ch, th and ng
structures.title: Adjacent consonants in words with sh, ch, th or ng
structures.explanation: A digraph is still one sound: in chest, ch is one sound and s-t are two. Count the sounds, then blend: ch-e-s-t, four sounds.

structures.label: With long vowel sounds
structures.title: Adjacent consonants in words with long vowel sounds
structures.explanation: The vowel digraph is one sound: tr-ai-n is four sounds, t-r-ai-n. Spot the digraph first, then blend every sound.

structures.label: Three consonants together
structures.title: Three consonant sounds together
structures.explanation: Some words start with three consonant sounds: s-t-r in strap, s-p-l in split. Each is its own sound; say all three, then blend.

structures.label: Longer and compound words
structures.title: Longer words and compound words
structures.explanation: Two short words joined together (farm + yard) or a longer word in two beats. Find the chunks, read each one, then blend them together.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ai' in rain — 'ay' is usually used at the end of a word, like day and play.
gpcs.mnemonic: When the /ai/ sound comes at the end of a word, it packs its bags and wears its 'y' boots instead of its 'i' coat. Sunbeam Day always waves goodbye with a big 'ay!' as the sun goes down.

character.name: Sunbeam Day
character.blurb: Sunbeam Day is the last warm ray of sunshine at the end of a bright day, and she only ever appears at the end of a word, just like 'ay'.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'y', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children stretch both arms up like sun rays, then swoop them down and out to the side while saying 'ay!' as if waving the day goodbye.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ow' in cow — 'ou' usually appears in the middle of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Boomer Cloud can't help it — every time he bumps into another cloud he lets out a great big 'ou!' that rumbles right across the sky.

character.name: Boomer Cloud
character.blurb: Boomer Cloud is a big grumbly cloud with one dark stripe across his middle, and he booms out 'ou' whenever he bumps into his friends.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'u', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children cup their hands round their mouth and call 'ou!' loudly like they're shouting across a playground.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'igh' in night — 'ie' often appears at the end of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Clyde Owl only opens his big eyes at night, and when he does he blinks twice and hoots a soft 'ie'.

character.name: Clyde Owl
character.blurb: Clyde Owl has one soft feather tuft standing up between his round eyes, and he only calls out at night, just like the sound hiding inside 'ie'.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children blink both eyes slowly, twice, while saying 'ie' softly like a sleepy owl.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ee' in tree — 'ea' is very common in the middle of words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Minty Leaf grows on the tea bush, and when the wind blows through her she rustles out a long 'ea, ea' sound.

character.name: Minty Leaf
character.blurb: Minty Leaf is a fresh green leaf from the tea bush, and she whispers 'ea' whenever a breeze passes through the branches.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'a', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children mime picking a leaf and holding it near their lips, then blow gently while saying 'ea' in a long stretched-out breath.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oi' in coin — 'oy' is usually used at the end of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Joy Butterfly can't sit still — whenever she finds a new flower she loops in the air and calls out 'oy!' with delight.

character.name: Joy Butterfly
character.blurb: Joy Butterfly has bright coral wings dotted with spots, and she calls out 'oy' whenever something makes her happy, always at the end of her little song.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'y', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children throw both arms up in a cheer and jump once, calling 'oy!' like they've just spotted a friend.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ur' in burn — 'ir' often appears in the middle of a word, right inside the word 'bird' itself.
gpcs.mnemonic: Twirl the Wren spins in a tight little circle on her branch and hums a low 'ir' as she turns.

character.name: Twirl the Wren
character.blurb: Twirl the Wren has one teal tuft on her head and loves to spin round and round on the spot, humming 'ir' the whole time.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children put one finger up and spin slowly on the spot, humming 'ir' until they stop.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon — 'ue' usually appears at the end of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Dewey Raindrop streaks down the window pane leaving a shiny trail and a soft 'ue' as he goes.

character.name: Dewey Raindrop
character.blurb: Dewey Raindrop is a sky-blue drop with one shiny streak down his middle, and he trails a long 'ue' sound as he slides.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children trace a finger down an imaginary window pane while saying a long 'ue' sound.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'or' in for — 'aw' usually appears at the end of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Hawthorn Hedgehog stretches out one spiky claw and scrapes it slowly along the ground, saying 'aw' as he goes.

character.name: Hawthorn Hedgehog
character.blurb: Hawthorn Hedgehog has sandy spines dotted with little spots, and he drags one claw along the path, saying 'aw' with every scrape.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children curl one hand into a claw shape and scrape it slowly through the air, saying 'aw'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Another way to write the /ch/ sound children already know from 'chip' — the t is silent. 'tch' comes straight after a short vowel at the end of a word: catch, fetch, kitchen. (Common exceptions: rich, which, much, such.)
gpcs.mnemonic: Catch it at the end: after a short vowel, /ch/ is usually spelt t-c-h, as in catch, fetch and kitchen.
gpcs.formation_cue: Write 't', then 'c', then 'h', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children pretend to catch a ball with both hands, saying 'ch' as they catch it.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'w' in web — the 'h' stays silent and mostly tags along in question words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Whisper the Feather floats wherever the wind takes her, asking a soft 'wh, wh' as she drifts past.

character.name: Whisper the Feather
character.blurb: Whisper the Feather is a pale sky-coloured feather who drifts on the breeze, whispering 'wh' every time the wind changes.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'w', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children blow softly onto their open hand, as if blowing a feather, while whispering 'wh'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'f' in fan — 'ph' often appears in longer, more grown-up words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Delphine Pinecone rattles her scales together and puffs out a breathy 'ph' whenever she's asked a question, as if she's answering the phone.

character.name: Delphine Pinecone
character.blurb: Delphine Pinecone is a deep berry-coloured pinecone speckled with spots, and she puffs a soft 'ph' sound out through her scales.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'p', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children hold a flat hand near their mouth like a phone and puff out a soft 'ph' sound.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: The /v/ sound children already know from 'van'. English words hardly ever end in the letter v, so when a word ends with a /v/ sound, an e is added after the v and makes no sound: give, live, have, sleeve.
gpcs.mnemonic: No word likes to end in v, so an e comes along to finish it — give, live, sleeve. Even Olive's name ends this way.
gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'v', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children rest two fingers on their lips and buzz 'vvv', then flick the fingers away for the quiet e.

trickyWords.tip: Made of two words joined together — 'to' plus 'day' — so once you know both halves, the whole word falls into place.
The 'ay' doesn't say its usual sound here — this word rhymes with 'fez', not with 'days', even though it's the family word for 'say'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon — 'ew' usually appears at the end of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Grew the Seed pushes up out of the soil a little further every day, stretching out a long 'ew' as he grows.

character.name: Grew the Seed
character.blurb: Grew the Seed is a small leaf-green seed who stretches taller each morning, humming 'ew' as he unfurls.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children start crouched low then slowly stretch upward with arms reaching, saying a long 'ew' as they rise.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oa' in boat — 'oe' is a less common ending used in only a handful of words.
gpcs.mnemonic: Rowan Duckling waddles along on her webbed toes, saying a rounded 'oe' with every step.

character.name: Rowan Duckling
character.blurb: Rowan Duckling has bright sunflower-yellow feathers and waddles along on webbed feet, calling 'oe' as she paddles.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children waddle in place with feet turned slightly out, saying 'oe' with each waddling step.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'or' in for and 'aw' in saw — 'au' usually appears in the middle of a word.
gpcs.mnemonic: Augustus Acorn drops from the branch every autumn with a soft thud and a low 'au' as he lands.

character.name: Augustus Acorn
character.blurb: Augustus Acorn wears one sandy stripe across his cap, and he only falls in autumn, landing with a gentle 'au'.

gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'u', close together — two letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children raise one hand high like a branch and let it drop slowly to their side, saying 'au' as it lands.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ai' in rain and 'ay' in day — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
gpcs.mnemonic: Echo Star sits at the far end of the word and can't shout her own name — instead she beams her light back over the consonant in between to wake up the 'a' and make it say its own name, 'ay'.

character.name: Echo Star
character.blurb: Echo Star sits quietly at the end of the word, and instead of making her own sound, she beams her light backwards to wake the letter across the gap.

gpcs.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'a', then a consonant in the middle, then 'e' right at the end — like cake, where 'a' and 'e' are two ends of a bridge with 'k' standing on it.
gpcs.action: Children point to an imaginary letter far ahead, then mime a beam travelling backward from their fingertip to their other hand, saying 'ay' as it arrives.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Another way to write the /air/ sound children already know from 'chair'. Say it the same way as 'air': care, share, scared.
gpcs.mnemonic: Take care and share: a-r-e can say /air/, just like the air in chair.
gpcs.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'r', then 'e', close together — three letters, one sound.
gpcs.action: Children hold out both hands as if sharing something with a friend, saying 'air'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ee' in tree and 'ea' in tea — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
gpcs.mnemonic: Evie Egg waits quietly at the end of the word, and when it's time she rolls her sound back over the consonant to wake up the 'e' at the front so it says its own name, 'ee'.

character.name: Evie Egg
character.blurb: Evie Egg sits at the end of the word like a small egg tucked at the end of a nest, sending her sound back across the gap to her matching 'e'.

gpcs.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'e', then a consonant, then 'e' again at the end — like these, where the two 'e's sit at opposite ends holding the middle letters between them.
gpcs.action: Children hold their hands far apart, then bring them together slowly while saying a long 'ee', as if the two ends are calling to each other.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'igh' in night and 'ie' in tie — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
gpcs.mnemonic: Skye Star twinkles at the end of the word and calls her sound back across the gap so the 'i' at the front can say its own name, like looking up and saying 'I see a star!'

character.name: Skye Star
character.blurb: Skye Star is speckled with little spots of light, and she twinkles at the end of the word, calling back to wake the 'i' at the front.

gpcs.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'i' with its dot, then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like time, where 'i' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letters like two stars at opposite ends of the sky.
gpcs.action: Children look up and point to the sky, then trace a line from their pointing finger back down to their chest while saying 'i' like naming themselves.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oa' in boat and 'oe' in toe — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
gpcs.mnemonic: Hollow the Nest sits snug at the end of the word, and she calls softly back over the consonant so the 'o' at the front says its own name, 'oh', like calling everyone home.

character.name: Hollow the Nest
character.blurb: Hollow the Nest is a cosy little nest lined with one soft tuft of moss, and she calls back across the word to bring the 'o' safely home.

gpcs.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'o', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like home, where 'o' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same nest.
gpcs.action: Children cup both hands together like a little nest, then slowly pull them apart while saying 'oh', as if opening the nest to let the sound out.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon (and sometimes sounds like 'you', as in cube) — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
gpcs.mnemonic: Tuney Bee hums her favourite tune at the end of the word, sending her buzz back over the consonant so the 'u' at the front wakes up and says its own name, 'you'.

character.name: Tuney Bee
character.blurb: Tuney Bee has berry-dark stripes and loves to hum, sending her buzzing sound back across the word to wake the 'u' at the front.

gpcs.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'u', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like cube, where 'u' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same tune.
gpcs.action: Children cup a hand behind their ear as if listening for a tune, then hum 'u' softly while bringing the hand forward.

trickyWords.tip: The 'ou' is the tricky part: it doesn't say any of its usual sounds here. Sound out the rest and remember that part.
The single letter 'y' at the end says /igh/, like in 'my' and 'try' — not its sometimes-/ee/ sound.
The 'ere' ending says /eer/ — it's the exact same letters as the ending of 'there' and 'where', but those two sound the same as each other while 'here' sounds different.
Starts with 'wh' saying /w/, then the 'ere' ending says /air/ — same spelling as 'here', a different sound.
The 'o' says /u/ and the 'e' on the end is silent — it rhymes with 'glove' and 'dove', not with 'move'.

alts.teaching_note: At the end of a short word, 'y' can say the same sound as 'igh' in 'light'. Try it in: my, by, fly, cry, try, shy.

alts.taught_as: /y/ as in yes, yak, yellow; also /igh/ as in my, fly
alts.teaching_note: At the end of a LONGER word, 'y' usually says /ee/ instead. Compare a short word ('my') with a longer one ('happy') to hear the difference.
After a 'w', 'a' can say /o/ instead of its usual short sound. Listen for it in: was, what, want, wash, wasp, swan.
On its own at the end of a tiny word, 'e' can say its long name-sound /ee/. Try: he, me, she, be, we.
Before 'nd', 'i' often says its long name-sound /igh/ instead of the short sound. Try: find, mind, kind, behind, blind.
On its own at the end of a word, 'o' can say its long name-sound /oa/. Try: go, no, so, zero.

alts.taught_as: /o/ as in dog, hot, top; also /oa/ as in go, no
alts.teaching_note: Sometimes 'o' says /u/ instead of either of its other sounds — these just have to be heard and remembered. Try: son, mother, come, love, some.
After certain letters, 'u' can say the short /oo/ sound instead. Try: put, full, pull, push, bull.

alts.taught_as: /u/ as in sun, cup, mud; also /oo/ as in put, full
alts.teaching_note: At the start of some words, 'u' says /yoo/ — like the letter's own name. Try: unicorn, unit, uniform, universe.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'c' usually says /s/ instead of /k/. Try: cent, city, ice, fence, pencil.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'g' can say /j/ instead of /g/. Try: giant, gem, cage, stage.
In some words (often borrowed from other languages), 'ch' says /k/ instead. Try: school, chorus, echo, Christmas, stomach.

alts.taught_as: /ch/ as in chip, chat, much; also /k/ as in school
alts.teaching_note: In a few other borrowed words, 'ch' says /sh/ instead. Try: chef, machine, chalet, moustache.
The same two letters 'ow' can also say /oa/, like in 'go'. Try: snow, grow, own, slow, window.
In the middle of some words, 'ie' says /ee/ instead of /igh/. Try: field, chief, thief, shield, believe.

trickyWords.tip: The whole word starts with a /w/ sound hidden inside the letter 'o', and the 'c' before the silent 'e' says /s/.
In southern British English the 'a' says /ar/ here instead of its usual short sound — read it left to right, a-s-k, and keep the sounds in that order.
The 'ie' in the middle says /e/ here, not its usual /ee/ or /igh/ sound — this word rhymes with 'bend', not with 'bead'.
The 'ch' says /k/ here, like a hard c, and the 'oo' keeps its long sound — the whole word reads 's-k-oo-l'.

alts.teaching_note: In a group of words, 'ea' says the short sound /e/ instead of /ee/. Try: head, bread, spread, instead, breakfast.
In a few words, 'ou' says the long /oo/ sound instead. Try: soup, group, you, route, youth.

alts.taught_as: /ow/ as in out, loud, round; also /oo/ as in soup, you
alts.teaching_note: In another small group, 'ou' says the short /u/ sound. Try: young, touch, country, double, cousin.
In some words, 'ear' says /er/ instead of /ear/ — there's no simple rule for which, so these are best learned as a small group. Try: earn, learn, early, pearl, heard.

alts.taught_as: /ear/ as in hear, year, dear; also /er/ as in learn, early
alts.teaching_note: 'ear' can also say /air/, the same sound as in 'chair' — in a small set of everyday words: bear, pear, wear, tear (as in tear a page). Read the word both ways and choose the one that makes sense.
Straight after a 'w', 'or' says /er/ instead of /or/. Try: word, work, world, worm, worth.
Four letters, one sound — 'eigh' says /ai/, the same sound already known from 'rain' and 'day'.
Without the silent 'gh', 'ei' can say the same /ai/ sound on its own.
At the end of a word, 'ey' most often says /ee/ (like 'key' or 'monkey'). In a smaller group of words it says /ai/ instead (like 'they' or 'grey') — point out both when they come up.
At the end of a word, 'ore' says /or/ — the same sound already known from 'for', spelled with a silent 'e' on the end.
A small group of words spell /or/ with 'oor' instead.
Another way to spell /or/ — say it as /or/, not as the 'ou' sound in 'out'.

trickyWords.tip: The 'ou' says its usual /ow/ sound, but the silent 'e' on the end does nothing you'd expect — it's just part of the word's shape.
The 'our' is the tricky part: here it doesn't say the sound you'd predict from the letters. Point to it and remember it.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say a soft hiss /s/ after sounds like p, t, k, f (cats); say a soft buzz /z/ after most other sounds, including vowels (dogs, runs).
gpcs.mnemonic: Ess the Seed-Pip lands on the end of a word to show there's more than one, or that it's happening right now — listen for his soft hiss or buzz.

character.name: Ess the Seed-Pip
character.blurb: A tiny seed-pip who hops onto the end of words, landing so softly he only ever adds a hiss or a buzz, never a whole new word.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-s' straight onto most root words with no change (cat→cats). If the word already ends in a hissing or buzzing letter string — s, x, sh, ch or ss — use '-es' instead.
gpcs.action: Wiggle one finger, then suddenly flash all five, to show 'one becomes many'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say it as a whole extra syllable, 'iz', so the word gets one more beat you can clap — box becomes two claps: box-es.
gpcs.mnemonic: Ezra the Bee always adds his own buzzing beat — '-es' — onto words that already end in a hiss, like box or bus.

character.name: Ezra the Bee
character.blurb: A busy bee who buzzes in with an extra beat whenever a word already ends in a hiss, so we can hear the ending properly.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-es' (not just '-s') when the root word ends in s, ss, x, ch or sh — it makes a whole new beat you can hear and clap: box→boxes, bus→buses, dish→dishes.
gpcs.action: Cup a hand behind your ear and add a little extra nod, as if catching the extra beat.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say the 'ng' sound through your nose at the end, like the middle of 'sing' — don't say 'in' or 'een'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Inga the Butterfly is always mid-flutter — add '-ing' to show an action is happening this very moment.

character.name: Inga the Butterfly
character.blurb: A butterfly who never sits still — she's always mid-flutter, which is why she loves showing off actions happening right now.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-ing' straight on for most words (jump→jumping). Drop a silent 'e' first (make→making). Double a short-vowel-plus-consonant ending first (run→running).
gpcs.action: Jog on the spot with arms pumping, to show the action happening right now.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: It can sound like /t/ (jumped), /d/ (played), or a whole extra beat /ɪd/ (wanted) — listen to the sound the root word ends in to know which.
gpcs.mnemonic: Eddy the Snail leaves his trail behind him — add '-ed' to show something already happened.

character.name: Eddy the Snail
character.blurb: A slow, thoughtful snail who always leaves a shiny trail behind him, showing where he has already been.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-ed' straight on for most words (jump→jumped). Drop a silent 'e' first (like→liked). Double a short-vowel-plus-consonant ending first (stop→stopped). A few words change completely instead (go→went) — these are learned separately as tricky past tenses.
gpcs.action: Point back over your shoulder with your thumb, to show the action is already behind you.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say a short, clear 'un' — the stress usually stays on the main word behind it, not on 'un-' itself.
gpcs.mnemonic: Una the Owl perches right at the front of a word and turns its meaning the opposite way round.

character.name: Una the Owl
character.blurb: A wise owl who can turn her head almost all the way round, always ready to flip things the opposite way.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add 'un-' to the very front of a whole word, with no changes to the root word underneath it: happy→unhappy, do→undo, pack→unpack.
gpcs.action: Cross both arms into an X in front of your chest, then snap them open, to show 'the opposite'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say a short, clear 'dis' with a soft hiss on the end — the stress usually stays on the main word behind it.
gpcs.mnemonic: Diz the Hedgehog sits at the front of a word and curls it up into its opposite.

character.name: Diz the Hedgehog
character.blurb: A small, prickly hedgehog who curls into a tight ball whenever he wants to say 'no thank you, not that'.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add 'dis-' to the very front of a whole word, with no changes to the root word underneath it: agree→disagree, appear→disappear, like→dislike.
gpcs.action: Curl into a small ball on the floor, then slowly uncurl while shaking your head 'no'.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say a soft, relaxed 'uh' sound at the end — in most British accents you won't hear a strong 'r'.
gpcs.mnemonic: Erno the Acorn loves comparing — add '-er' to say one thing is more than another, or to name someone who does something.

character.name: Erno the Acorn
character.blurb: A proud little acorn who's always comparing himself to the acorn next to him, hoping to grow just a bit bigger.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-er' straight on for most words (fast→faster). Drop a silent 'e' first (large→larger). Double a short-vowel-plus-consonant ending first (big→bigger). To mean 'a person who does this', add '-er' to an action word (run→runner).
gpcs.action: Stand on tiptoes and stretch one hand a little higher than the other.

gpcs.pronunciation_note: Say a clear extra beat, 'ist', at the end — it always adds a whole new syllable you can clap.
gpcs.mnemonic: Essie the Sunflower stretches up taller than all the rest — add '-est' when something is the most, out of everyone.

character.name: Essie the Sunflower
character.blurb: A sunflower who stretches taller than every other flower in the patch, always reaching to be the very best.

gpcs.formation_cue: Add '-est' straight on for most words (fast→fastest). Drop a silent 'e' first (large→largest). Double a short-vowel-plus-consonant ending first (big→biggest).
gpcs.action: Stand on tiptoes and stretch both hands as high as they'll go, higher than everyone else.

year2.focus: Review of Phase 5, and Year 1's extra ways to spell and say sounds; begin Year 2 common exception words (first third of the 64-word list) alongside daily reading and spelling practice. Year 2 spellings in National Curriculum Appendix 1 start here, e.g. /ee/ spelt ey (key, donkey, monkey).
Continue Year 2 common exception words (second third); introduce the Year 2 suffix rules (-ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly) and the spelling patterns for adding -ed/-ing to longer words.
Finish Year 2 common exception words (final third); homophone awareness (e.g. there/their/they're) using only GPCs already taught; continuing fluency practice with phase-matched books.

Review across the full code (Phases 2-6, including Year 1's extra ways to spell and say sounds); targeted Fast Track for anyone who did not meet the Year 1 PSC standard, run alongside the mainstream Year 2 spelling curriculum.
Year 2 retake of the Phonics Screening Check for any child who did not meet the standard in Year 1 — same PSC-review approach as Year 1 Summer 1, individually targeted.
Consolidation and transition to Year 3 spelling expectations; fluency and comprehension take over as the main focus once decoding is secure.
